quests.question: What the researchers discovered ___ remarkable.
quests.hint: A subject clause starting with 'what' is treated as singular.
quests.explanation: A 'what' clause acting as the subject is always singular. 'What the researchers discovered was remarkable' - it functions as a single noun phrase.

quests.question: What the children need most ___ love and stability.
quests.hint: The subject clause 'What the children need most' is treated as singular.
quests.explanation: A subject clause beginning with 'what' is singular. 'What the children need most is love and stability' - the verb is 'is', not 'are'.

quests.question: What the critics said about the film ___ mostly positive.
quests.hint: The 'what' clause ('What the critics said') is the subject - singular.
quests.explanation: The subject 'what the critics said' is a noun clause that acts as a singular unit. 'What the critics said was mostly positive'.

quests.question: Where the children play ___ completely safe.
quests.hint: A 'where' clause acting as the subject is treated as singular.
quests.explanation: A subject clause beginning with 'where' is treated as a singular noun phrase. 'Where the children play is completely safe'.

quests.question: Why she left the company ___ still unclear.
quests.hint: A 'why' clause acting as the subject is treated as singular.
quests.explanation: Subject clauses beginning with 'why', 'where', 'when', or 'how' are always singular. 'Why she left is still unclear'.

quests.question: How the accident happened ___ still being investigated.
quests.hint: A 'how' clause as the subject is always singular.
quests.explanation: A 'how' clause acting as subject is treated as a singular noun phrase. 'How the accident happened is still being investigated'.

quests.question: The reason the bridge collapsed ___ still under investigation.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the reason' (singular) - the embedded clause doesn't change that.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the reason'. The embedded clause 'the bridge collapsed' explains the reason but does not affect the verb. 'The reason is still under investigation'.

quests.question: The fact that many students struggle with maths ___ well documented.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the fact' (singular) - the 'that' clause is an appositive.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the fact'. The 'that' clause ('that many students struggle with maths') expands on it but doesn't change agreement. 'The fact is well documented'.

quests.question: The idea that stress ___ learning is widely accepted.
quests.hint: Inside the 'that' clause, 'stress' is singular - the verb inside agrees with it.
quests.explanation: Inside the embedded clause 'that stress affects learning', the subject is 'stress', which is singular. The verb inside the clause is 'affects'.

quests.question: The suggestion that employees ___ more breaks was rejected.
quests.hint: Inside the 'that' clause, 'employees' is plural - verb inside the clause agrees.
quests.explanation: Inside the embedded clause 'that employees take more breaks', the subject is 'employees', which is plural. The verb inside is 'take'.

quests.question: It ___ known that high-intensity exercise has many benefits.
quests.hint: 'It' as a subject is always singular, even in impersonal constructions.
quests.explanation: In impersonal constructions ('it is known that...'), 'it' is always singular. 'It is known that...' is the correct form.

quests.question: It ___ the long hours that made the job so stressful.
quests.hint: In this cleft sentence, 'it' is always singular.
quests.explanation: In cleft sentences ('it was/were... that'), 'it' takes a singular verb. 'It was the long hours that made the job stressful' is standard.

quests.question: Making mistakes ___ part of the learning process.
quests.hint: A gerund phrase as subject is always singular.
quests.explanation: 'Making mistakes' is a gerund phrase acting as the subject. Gerund phrases are always singular: 'making mistakes is part of the process'.

quests.question: Accepting criticism and learning from it ___ essential skills.
quests.hint: Two gerund phrases connected by 'and' - count them as a plural subject.
quests.explanation: 'Accepting criticism' and 'learning from it' are two distinct activities. Two gerund phrases joined by 'and' always take a plural verb: 'are essential skills'.

quests.question: The number of hours she works each week ___ astonishing.
quests.hint: 'The number of' is always singular - it refers to one total.
quests.explanation: 'The number of' is always singular. 'The number of hours is astonishing' - not 'are'. Compare with 'a number of hours are available'.

quests.question: She is one of those people who ___ everything personally.
quests.hint: Does the relative clause verb agree with 'one' or with 'people'?
quests.explanation: In 'one of those people who take things personally', the verb in the relative clause agrees with 'people' (plural), not 'one'. However, in informal English both 'takes' and 'take' are used - 'take' is the more careful grammatical choice.

quests.question: He is the only one of the applicants who ___ previous experience.
quests.hint: With 'the only one of', the relative clause verb agrees with 'one' (singular).
quests.explanation: With 'the only one of [plural noun] who', the verb agrees with 'one', not the plural noun. 'The only one who has experience' - singular, because only one person qualifies.

quests.question: Reading widely ___ the single best way to improve your vocabulary.
quests.hint: A gerund phrase ('Reading widely') as subject is singular.
quests.explanation: A gerund phrase as subject is always singular. 'Reading widely is the single best way' - the verb is 'is', not 'are'.

quests.question: The policy that was introduced last year ___ significant changes.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the policy' (singular) - the relative clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the policy'. The relative clause 'that was introduced last year' describes it but does not change agreement. 'The policy has brought significant changes'.

quests.question: The policies that were introduced last year ___ significant changes.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the policies' (plural) - relative clause doesn't change that.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the policies', which is plural. The relative clause 'that were introduced last year' describes them. 'The policies have brought significant changes'.

quests.question: Knowing when to speak and when to stay silent ___ a valuable skill.
quests.hint: Two infinitive-like phrases joined by 'and' can be treated as a single skill - singular.
quests.explanation: When two 'when to...' clauses describe a single ability, they are treated as one concept and take a singular verb: 'knowing when to speak and when to stay silent is a skill'.

quests.question: The evidence that scientists ___ collected suggests a clear link.
quests.hint: Inside the relative clause, 'that' refers to 'scientists' (plural).
quests.explanation: 'That' in the relative clause refers to 'scientists', which is plural. So the verb inside the clause is 'have': 'that scientists have collected'.

quests.question: The evidence that ___ presented during the trial is now disputed.
quests.hint: Inside the relative clause, 'that' refers to 'the evidence' (uncountable, singular).
quests.explanation: 'That' refers to 'the evidence', which is uncountable and singular. The verb inside the clause is 'was': 'the evidence that was presented during the trial'.

quests.question: What she told me about the project ___ very encouraging.
quests.hint: The 'what' clause acting as subject is always singular.
quests.explanation: 'What she told me about the project' is a noun clause functioning as the singular subject. 'What she told me was very encouraging'.

quests.question: The team that has trained the longest ___ at an advantage.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the team' (singular) - relative clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the team', a singular collective. The relative clause 'that has trained the longest' describes it. 'The team is at an advantage'.

quests.question: Neither of the proposals that were submitted ___ approved.
quests.hint: 'Neither of' with a relative clause - the subject is still 'neither' (singular in formal English).
quests.explanation: The subject is 'neither of the proposals', which is singular in formal English. 'Neither of the proposals was approved' - singular verb in careful writing.

quests.question: To make decisions under pressure ___ a crucial leadership skill.
quests.hint: The infinitive phrase 'To make decisions under pressure' is the subject - singular.
quests.explanation: An infinitive phrase acting as subject is always singular. 'To make decisions under pressure is a crucial leadership skill'.

quests.question: The way computers process data ___ changed enormously in recent years.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the way' (singular) - the embedded clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: 'The way' is the singular subject. The clause 'computers process data' tells us more about the way, but 'the way has changed' is correct - singular verb.

quests.question: What parents want most for their children ___ a safe and happy life.
quests.hint: The 'what' clause is the subject - treated as a singular noun phrase.
quests.explanation: The subject 'what parents want most for their children' is a noun clause acting as a singular unit. 'What parents want most is a safe and happy life'.

quests.question: The fact that both candidates ___ qualified makes the choice difficult.
quests.hint: Inside the 'that' clause, 'both candidates' is plural - verb inside agrees.
quests.explanation: Inside the embedded clause 'that both candidates are qualified', the subject is 'both candidates', which is plural. The verb inside the clause is 'are'.
